also_built_by: Noorduyn, Canadian Car and Foundry, Commonwealth Aircraft Corporation
description:
The T-6 Texan is a single-engine advanced trainer developed by North American Aviation from the NA-16 prototype first flown in April 1935. It was built to bridge the gap between basic trainers and frontline combat types, carrying retractable landing gear, a variable-pitch propeller and provision for gunnery and instrument instruction.

The type entered US Army Air Corps service in 1937 and served the US Navy as the SNJ and Commonwealth air forces as the Harvard, becoming the standard advanced trainer of the British Commonwealth Air Training Plan. Production reached 15,495 aircraft, and more than 60 air forces operated it. Armed examples flew forward air control missions in Korea and counter-insurgency sorties elsewhere; the South African Air Force retired the last military examples in 1995.

The direct-drive Pratt & Whitney R-1340 drives propeller tips to near-sonic speed, producing the rasping note the type is known for. Large postwar surplus stocks explain its continued presence in collections.
engines: 1 x Pratt & Whitney R-1340-AN-1 Wasp radial

description:
The Meteor was the first British jet fighter and the only Allied jet to fly combat operations in the Second World War. Designed by George Carter at Gloster to Specification F9/40, it used two centrifugal-flow turbojets mounted in mid-wing nacelles, an arrangement chosen because early engines could not deliver enough thrust singly.

No. 616 Squadron received the first aircraft in July 1944 and used them against V-1 flying bombs. Meteors set world air speed records in 1945 and 1946, and the F.8 became the principal day-fighter version. Australian No. 77 Squadron flew them in Korea against the MiG-15, which outclassed them at altitude. Radar-equipped NF night fighters and PR reconnaissance versions followed. Of 3,947 built, exports went to Argentina, Egypt, Israel, Denmark and others; RAF target tugs flew until 1982.

The straight wing and wide engine nacelles mark it as a first-generation jet.

also_built_by: de Havilland Canada, de Havilland Australia, de Havilland New Zealand, Morris Motors, OGMA
description:
The DH.82 Tiger Moth is a two-seat biplane primary trainer developed by de Havilland from the DH.60 Moth and first flown in October 1931. The upper wing was swept back and moved forward relative to the lower to clear the front cockpit, allowing an instructor wearing a parachute to escape from the enclosed forward position.

It entered RAF service in February 1932 and became the standard elementary trainer of the RAF and Commonwealth air forces, including the British Commonwealth Air Training Plan. In 1940 some flew coastal patrols and were fitted to carry light bombs. Production totalled 8,868, with licence and subcontract assembly in Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Portugal, Norway and Sweden. RAF service ended in 1959, after which surplus airframes passed into civil flying, crop dusting and aerial topdressing.

The pronounced wing stagger and inverted Gipsy Major engine distinguish it from earlier Moths.
engines: 1 x de Havilland Gipsy Major I inverted inline

description:
The Jaguar is a twin-engine supersonic ground attack aircraft produced by SEPECAT, a joint venture formed in 1966 between the British Aircraft Corporation and Breguet. It began as a combined British and French requirement for an advanced trainer with light attack capability, but grew into a low-level tactical strike and reconnaissance aircraft with a nuclear delivery role for both nations.

It entered service in 1973 with the RAF and the Armee de l'Air. French Jaguars flew operations over Mauritania, Chad and Iraq; RAF aircraft flew in the 1991 Gulf War, over Bosnia and in the Iraqi no-fly zones. Exports went to Oman, Ecuador and Nigeria, and Hindustan Aeronautics built the type under licence in India as the Shamsher. Of 573 built, France retired its fleet in 2005, Britain in 2007 and Oman in 2014; India still operates the type.

The shoulder-mounted wing, tall twin-wheel landing gear and overwing missile pylons are characteristic.
engines: 2 x Rolls-Royce Turbomeca Adour Mk.102 afterburning turbofans

also_built_by: SABCA, Fokker, TUSAS, Korea Aerospace Industries
description:
The F-16 is a single-engine multirole fighter designed by General Dynamics for the US Air Force Lightweight Fighter programme, the YF-16 prototype flying in 1974 and winning the competition against the YF-17 in 1975. It was the first production fighter built with relaxed static stability and fly-by-wire controls, combined with a frameless bubble canopy, a reclined ejection seat and a sidestick controller.

It entered USAF service in 1978 and was selected in the same period by Belgium, Denmark, the Netherlands and Norway to replace the F-104. Israeli F-16s struck the Osirak reactor in 1981 and claimed numerous kills over Lebanon in 1982; the type flew in the Gulf War, the Balkans, Iraq, Afghanistan and Libya. Some 4,600 have been built, with licence assembly in Belgium, the Netherlands, Turkey and South Korea, and production continues as the F-16V Block 70.

The single ventral intake below the cockpit identifies it at a distance.
engines: 1 x General Electric F110-GE-129 afterburning turbofan

description:
The MiG-29 is a twin-engine air-superiority fighter developed by the Mikoyan design bureau from the Soviet PFI requirement issued in 1969, which sought a light frontal-aviation counterpart to the American F-15 and F-16. Detailed design work began in 1974 and the prototype flew on 6 October 1977.

It entered Soviet service in August 1983 and was widely exported, serving with more than 30 air forces including India, Poland, Iraq, Cuba and Algeria. More than 1,600 were built before Russian production ended in 2019. Reunified Germany inherited East German aircraft and flew them until 2004. The type has seen combat from the 1991 Gulf War and the Kosovo conflict to the fighting in Ukraine.

Large curved leading-edge root extensions blend the wings into the fuselage, and louvred doors close the main intakes during takeoff, air being drawn instead through openings in the upper wing roots.

also_built_by: English Electric, SNCASE, Fiat, Macchi, Commonwealth Aircraft Corporation, Swiss Federal Aircraft Factory, Hindustan Aircraft
description:
The Vampire is a single-engine jet fighter designed by de Havilland from a 1941 specification and built around the Halford H.1 turbojet, later named Goblin. Its twin-boom layout kept the jet pipe short, limiting thrust loss from the low-powered early engine. The prototype flew on 20 September 1943.

It entered RAF service in 1946 as the service's second jet fighter and in 1948 became the first jet aircraft to cross the Atlantic. Frontline RAF use ended in 1953, after which it flew in ground-attack and training roles until 1966. Thirty-one air forces operated the type, which saw action in the Malayan Emergency, at Suez and in Rhodesia. 3,268 were built in Britain and 1,512 abroad under licence; Switzerland retired the last in 1990.

The fuselage pod is a moulded plywood and balsa shell in de Havilland Mosquito practice, with only the booms and wings in metal.
engines: 1 x de Havilland Goblin 3 centrifugal-flow turbojet

description:
The L-39 Albatros is a two-seat jet trainer designed by Aero Vodochody under Jan Vlcek as a successor to the L-29 Delfin. It first flew on 4 November 1968 and was the first trainer aircraft built around a turbofan powerplant, the Soviet-supplied Ivchenko AI-25TL.

It entered Czechoslovak service in March 1972 and was adopted by most Warsaw Pact air forces as their standard jet trainer. About 2,900 were built between 1971 and 1996, serving more than 30 air forces. The armed L-39ZO and L-39ZA versions added four underwing pylons and a GSh-23 cannon and flew light-attack missions in Afghanistan, Libya, Syria and Ukraine.

Surplus airframes are common in civilian hands; simple systems and comparatively low operating costs have made the L-39 the most numerous privately owned jet warbird.

The OH-6 Cayuse is a light observation helicopter designed by Hughes as the Model 369 to meet a 1960 US Army requirement to replace the Bell H-13 Sioux. It first flew on 27 February 1963 and won the Light Observation Helicopter competition against Bell and Fairchild-Hiller entries, with a production contract awarded in May 1965.

Deliveries to South Vietnam began in December 1967, where crews nicknamed it the Loach and paired it with AH-1 Cobra gunships in hunter-killer scout teams, the OH-6 flying low to draw fire and mark targets. Losses were heavy: 964 of the 1,420 US Army aircraft were destroyed. Hughes lost the follow-on contract to Bell's OH-58 in 1968, but Kawasaki built 387 under licence in Japan and the design continued as the civil Model 500.

The teardrop fuselage, internal bulkheads and self-sealing tanks gave unusual crash survivability.

The Su-7 is a single-seat swept-wing supersonic jet designed by the Sukhoi bureau, whose S-1 prototype flew on 7 September 1955. Intended as a low-level day fighter, it proved unsuited to that role; the Su-7B fighter-bomber derivative instead became the Soviet Union's principal ground-attack aircraft of the 1960s.

1,847 were built between 1957 and 1972. Exports went to India, Egypt, Syria, Iraq, Poland and Czechoslovakia among others, and the type fought in the 1967 Six-Day War, the War of Attrition, the 1973 Yom Kippur War and the 1971 Indo-Pakistani war, where Indian crews sustained high sortie rates and recovered badly damaged aircraft. The variable-geometry Su-17 replaced it in Soviet service.

The thirsty Lyulka AL-7F engine forced two of the four pylons to carry drop tanks on most sorties, sharply limiting the warload.

also_built_by: Fuji, Canadian Car and Foundry, FMA
description:
The T-34 Mentor is a two-seat primary trainer developed by Beechcraft as a private venture, adapting the structure of the Model 35 Bonanza to a tandem cockpit and conventional tail. It first flew on 2 December 1948, offering the US services a piston trainer with handling closer to the jets students would later fly.

The USAF adopted it as the T-34A in 1953 and the Navy as the T-34B. More than 2,300 were built, including 173 by Fuji in Japan, 125 by Canadian Car and Foundry and 75 by FMA in Argentina. A turboprop rebuild, the T-34C Turbo-Mentor, carried the design into Navy primary training until the T-6 Texan II replaced it.

The long single-piece canopy over stepped tandem seats distinguishes it from the Bonanza it derives from. Large numbers passed into civil hands, making it common on the warbird and aerobatic circuit.

The T-28 Trojan is a two-seat piston trainer designed by North American Aviation to replace the T-6 Texan. It first flew on 24 September 1949 and introduced a tricycle undercarriage, a stepped tandem cockpit and performance high enough to cover both primary and advanced training in one airframe.

The USAF took the 800 hp T-28A; the Navy's T-28B and carrier-capable T-28C used the 1,425 hp Wright R-1820 radial. Production ran to 1,948 aircraft between 1950 and 1957. Armed T-28D Nomad conversions flew counter-insurgency strike missions in Vietnam and Laos, and France rebuilt surplus airframes as the Fennec for use in Algeria. The Philippine Air Force retired the last military examples in 1994.

The oversized three-bladed propeller and deep radial cowling mark out the B and D models.

The O-1 Bird Dog is a single-engine liaison and observation aircraft derived from the Cessna 170. It first flew on 14 December 1949 and entered service in 1950 as the L-19, the first all-metal fixed-wing type ordered by the US Army after the 1947 reorganisation split the air arms. The requirement was battlefield observation, artillery spotting and light liaison from short unprepared strips.

Bird Dogs directed artillery in Korea and, in Vietnam, flew as forward air control aircraft marking targets with white phosphorus rockets for fast jets. Cessna built 3,431 and Fuji added 60 under licence in Japan; US military service ended in 1974, though export operators flew them far longer.

The deep wrap-around greenhouse glazing behind and above the cabin, giving near-unobstructed downward vision, is its defining feature.

The Jet Provost is a side-by-side two-seat jet basic trainer developed by Hunting Percival from the piston-engined Provost, replacing the radial engine with a Viper turbojet and adding a tricycle undercarriage. The prototype flew on 26 June 1954. It was built to test whether ab initio students could be taught on jets from the start rather than converting from pistons.

The RAF accepted the concept and the type became its standard basic trainer from 1955, serving until 1993 when the Shorts Tucano took over. A total of 734 were built, latterly by the British Aircraft Corporation. The armed Strikemaster development was exported widely for light attack.

The tall, spindly nose leg that gives the aircraft its nose-high ground stance was fitted so students had good forward vision while taxiing.
engines: 1 x Armstrong Siddeley Viper Mk.202 turbojet

description:
The Lynx is a twin-engined multi-purpose military helicopter designed by Westland under the 1967 Anglo-French helicopter agreement, in which Aerospatiale held a 30 per cent production share. It first flew on 21 March 1971 and was built in two families: a wheeled naval variant for frigate and destroyer decks, and a skid-equipped battlefield version for the British Army.

Naval Lynxes carried Sea Skua missiles and torpedoes, and sank or disabled several Iraqi vessels in the 1991 Gulf War; army machines flew anti-tank and utility work in Northern Ireland, the Balkans, Iraq and Afghanistan. Around 450 were built and exported to more than a dozen navies. British service ended in 2017-18, superseded by the Wildcat.

The semi-rigid titanium rotor head gave it unusual agility; a modified Lynx set the helicopter speed record of 400.87 km/h in 1986.

The CT-133 Silver Star is a two-seat jet trainer built by Canadair under a 1951 licence agreement covering the Lockheed T-33. The Canadian aircraft differs from the American original in its powerplant: a Rolls-Royce Nene 10 turbojet of 5,000 lbf in place of the Allison J33, giving more thrust and a deeper rear fuselage to accommodate it.

Canadair completed 656 airframes, the first flying in 1952. The type trained Royal Canadian Air Force and later Canadian Forces pilots until it was replaced in the advanced training role in 1976, then continued for three more decades in utility work: target towing, electronic threat simulation, pilot proficiency and communications flying. Final Canadian Forces examples were withdrawn in 2005. Aircraft were also supplied to Bolivia, France, Greece, Portugal and Turkey.

The straight wing with permanent tip tanks and the single dorsal intake distinguish it from swept-wing contemporaries.

The T-37 is a side-by-side twin-jet primary trainer developed by Cessna to a 1952 United States Air Force requirement for an aircraft that would take student pilots from their first flight into jets rather than beginning them on piston types. The design emphasised docile low-speed handling, short-field performance and simple maintenance, with the two small turbojets mounted in the wing roots and the crew seated low under a wide canopy.

The prototype flew on 12 October 1954 and the type entered service in 1957. Cessna built 1,269 aircraft, and the T-37 remained the USAF's basic jet trainer until 2009. Exports went to some two dozen air forces including Pakistan, Turkey, Germany, Greece, Colombia and Brazil. The armed A-37 Dragonfly derivative flew counter-insurgency missions in Vietnam.

The high-pitched shriek of its engines gave the type its Tweet nickname.

The G.91 is a single-seat light strike and reconnaissance fighter designed by Giuseppe Gabrielli at Fiat for the NATO NBMR-1 competition of 1953, which sought a cheap lightweight aircraft able to operate from damaged or unprepared airfields. The prototype first flew on 9 August 1956 and the design was declared the competition winner in January 1958, powered by a single Bristol Siddeley Orpheus turbojet.

Italy introduced the type operationally in 1961 and West Germany in 1962; German industry licence-built 294 aircraft. Total production reached 756 including the twin-engined G.91Y. Portugal flew 40 G.91R/4 aircraft in its African colonial wars between 1966 and 1974, losing several to SA-7 missiles. Italian service ended in 1995.

The nose bears a fighter-style intake and, on reconnaissance variants, oblique camera windows.

The Lightning is a supersonic interceptor designed by W. E. W. Petter's team at English Electric and later built by the British Aircraft Corporation. It was created to destroy high-altitude Soviet bombers approaching the United Kingdom, and its layout is unusual: two Rolls-Royce Avon turbojets stacked vertically in the fuselage, fed by a single nose intake with a conical shock centrebody, behind a sharply swept wing with a clipped, notched leading edge.

The P.1A prototype flew on 4 August 1954 and squadron service began on 11 July 1960. Performance was extreme for its generation, with Mach 2 speed and a climb rate that allowed zoom ascents above 60,000 feet, but internal fuel was small and endurance correspondingly short. 337 were built. Saudi Arabia and Kuwait were the only export customers. The RAF retired the type on 30 April 1988.

The F-105 is a single-seat supersonic fighter-bomber designed by Republic Aviation as a private venture to deliver a nuclear weapon carried in an internal bomb bay at low level and high speed. It was the largest single-engine, single-seat combat aircraft built for the United States Air Force, with a Pratt & Whitney J75 turbojet and distinctive forward-swept wing-root intakes. First flight was 22 October 1955 and service entry 27 May 1958.

In Vietnam the type flew the majority of strike missions over North Vietnam in the war's early years, some 20,000 sorties, and was credited with 27.5 aerial victories. Of 833 built, 395 were lost in Southeast Asia. Two-seat F-105F and F-105G Wild Weasel conversions pioneered suppression of enemy air defences. The last examples left Air Force Reserve and Air National Guard service on 25 February 1984.
engines: 1 x Pratt & Whitney J75-P-19W afterburning turbojet

description:
The P-51 Mustang is a single-seat fighter and fighter-bomber designed by North American Aviation in 1940 to a British Purchasing Commission requirement. The original Allison-engined version performed poorly at altitude; fitting the Rolls-Royce Merlin, built under licence by Packard as the V-1650, transformed it into a high-altitude escort fighter with the range to accompany heavy bombers from England to Berlin and back.

Mustangs served with the USAAF, RAF, RAAF, RCAF and RNZAF in Europe, the Mediterranean and the Pacific, then flew ground-attack missions in Korea as the F-51D. A total of 15,686 were built, with further licence production by Commonwealth Aircraft Corporation in Australia. The last military operator, the Dominican Air Force, retired its Mustangs in 1984.

The P-51D is identified by its bubble canopy, cut-down rear fuselage and the large ventral radiator scoop behind the cockpit that houses the Meredith-effect cooling duct.

The Su-22 is the export designation of the Sukhoi Su-17, a single-seat Soviet ground-attack aircraft developed from the fixed-wing Su-7. To improve short-field performance, the design bureau fitted variable-geometry outer wing panels while leaving the inner wing fixed, giving the type its distinctive part-swing wing. The prototype flew on 2 August 1966 and the aircraft entered Soviet service in 1970.

Export aircraft were designated Su-20 with downgraded avionics and Su-22 when fitted with the Tumansky R-29 engine for customers outside the Warsaw Pact. Some 2,867 were built. They flew combat with Soviet forces in Afghanistan, with Iraq against Iran, and with Libya, Syria, Peru and Vietnam. Russia withdrew its last Su-17M4 in 1998 and Poland retired its Su-22s in 2025, but a few remain in service elsewhere.

The fixed inner wing with pivoting outer panels and the tall dorsal spine distinguish it from the Su-7.

The MiG-19 is a twin-engine Soviet interceptor and day fighter, the first Soviet production aircraft capable of supersonic speed in level flight. It was developed by the Mikoyan-Gurevich bureau as a successor to the MiG-17, with swept wings, an all-moving tailplane and two Tumansky RD-9B afterburning turbojets. The SM-2 prototype flew on 24 May 1952 and the type entered service in March 1955.

Soviet production totalled 2,172 aircraft, with licence manufacture in Czechoslovakia as the Aero S-105 and in China as the Shenyang J-6, which was built in far larger numbers and exported widely. MiG-19s and J-6s flew in Vietnam, the Indo-Pakistani wars and the Iran-Iraq War, and intercepted reconnaissance aircraft over Soviet territory.

The type is recognised by its side-by-side engines, sharply swept wing with fences, and three 30 mm NR-30 cannon.

The CM.170 Magister is a two-seat French jet trainer, the first purpose-designed jet trainer to enter large-scale production. Design began at Etablissements Fouga in 1948 as a light jet primary trainer; after the French Air Force judged the initial proposal underpowered, the airframe was enlarged around two Turbomeca Marbore turbojets while keeping the butterfly tail of the earlier Fouga CM.8 glider. It first flew on 23 July 1952 and entered service in 1956.

A total of 868 were built: 576 in France, 194 in West Germany by Heinkel-Messerschmitt, 62 in Finland by Valmet and 36 in Israel by IAI. The carrier-capable CM.175 Zephyr served the French Navy. Israeli Magisters flew armed ground-attack sorties in the 1967 Six-Day War.

The V-shaped butterfly tail and slim wingtip fuel tanks make the type immediately identifiable.

The TS-11 Iskra is a Polish two-seat jet trainer designed by a team under Tadeusz Soltyk at PZL-Mielec to replace piston-engined trainers in Warsaw Pact service. It first flew on 5 February 1960 and uses a single indigenous WSK SO-3 turbojet mounted in the rear fuselage, with side intakes at the wing roots and a raised tandem cockpit. It entered Polish service in 1964.

Poland selected the Iskra for its own air force after the Warsaw Pact standardised on the Czechoslovak L-29 Delfin, making it the only member state to field a national design in the role. Production totalled 424 aircraft. Besides the Polish Air Force and Navy, the Indian Air Force operated 76. Armed reconnaissance variants carried a 23 mm cannon and underwing pylons. The type was retired in 2021.

The Polish aerobatic team Bialo-Czerwone Iskry flew it for decades.

The Mirage F1 is a single-engine multirole fighter designed by Dassault as a successor to the delta-winged Mirage III. It abandoned the delta for a swept, shoulder-mounted wing with full-span slats and double-slotted flaps, which shortened the takeoff run, improved low-level handling and allowed a large increase in internal fuel. The prototype flew on 23 December 1966 and the F1C entered French service in 1973 as an all-weather interceptor with Cyrano IV radar.

Production reached 726 aircraft, serving fourteen air forces including Spain, Greece, Morocco, Iraq, Libya, Kuwait, Jordan, Ecuador and South Africa. Iraqi F1EQs carried Exocet missiles during the Iran-Iraq War; other examples fought over Chad, Western Sahara and in the 1991 Gulf War. France withdrew its last F1CRs on 13 June 2014, though a few operators and civil contractors still fly the type.

The high-set wing and tall swept fin distinguish it from the earlier Mirage deltas, and two 30 mm DEFA cannon sit in the lower forward fuselage.

The Yak-40 is a three-engine short-haul airliner developed by the Yakovlev design bureau to replace piston types such as the Li-2 and An-2 on Aeroflot local services. The specification demanded safe operation from poorly equipped fields with unpaved runways under 700 m, which produced an unswept wing, a rear ventral airstair and three Ivchenko AI-25 turbofans grouped at the tail. It first flew on 21 October 1966 and entered Aeroflot service on 30 September 1968.

About 1,011 were built at Saratov between 1967 and 1981. It was the first Soviet airliner to gain Western airworthiness certification and was exported to some 22 countries in Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America, also serving as an air ambulance, survey platform and government transport.

The straight, untapered wing is unusual on a jet transport, and the centre engine exhausts through a reverser at the base of the fin.

Harvard is the British Commonwealth name for North American's advanced single-engine trainer, the aircraft the United States services called the T-6 Texan. It descended from the NA-16 of 1935 by way of the BC-1, and the RAF ordered it in 1938 as the Harvard I. Two crew sat in tandem under a long glazed canopy behind a 600 hp Pratt & Whitney R-1340 radial, with retractable undercarriage and flaps giving pupils the handling of a front-line fighter.

The type became the standard advanced trainer of the British Commonwealth Air Training Plan. The RAF took 430 Harvard Is and 1,275 Harvard IIs; from 1942 Noorduyn Aviation of Montreal built 2,557 Harvard IIBs, and Canadian Car and Foundry produced the postwar Harvard 4. The South African Air Force received well over a thousand and flew them until 1995, the last military operator.

The direct-drive propeller takes its tips supersonic, giving the type its distinctive rasping note.
engines: 1 x Pratt & Whitney R-1340-AN-1 Wasp radial

description:
The DC-3 is a twin-engine all-metal airliner built by Douglas after American Airlines asked for a sleeper version of the DC-2 to replace its Curtiss Condor biplanes. The Douglas Sleeper Transport flew on 17 December 1935, and the 21 to 32 seat day version followed. A cantilever wing, retractable undercarriage, controllable-pitch propellers and two 1,200 hp Pratt & Whitney R-1830 radials let an operator carry passengers at a profit without relying on mail contracts.

American opened Newark to Chicago services on 26 June 1936. Douglas completed 607 civil DC-3s before production turned to the military C-47; counting that aircraft and the licence-built Lisunov Li-2 and Showa L2D, 16,079 of the family were made. Surplus wartime transports converted to civil use kept the type on scheduled routes worldwide, and a small number still fly commercially.

The tailwheel undercarriage gives the fuselage its nose-high attitude on the ground.
engines: 2 x Pratt & Whitney R-1830 Twin Wasp radials

description:
The Tornado is a twin-engine, variable-geometry combat aircraft developed by Panavia Aircraft GmbH, a consortium formed in 1969 by Britain, West Germany and Italy to replace the F-104 Starfighter and Canberra with a single airframe. The interdictor strike version was built to penetrate at very low level in any weather using terrain-following radar, while the air defence variant served Britain as a long-range interceptor.

The first prototype flew on 14 August 1974 and the type entered service in 1979; 990 were completed by 1998, comprising 745 IDS, 194 ADV and 51 ECR aircraft. Operators were the RAF, the Luftwaffe and Marineflieger, Italy and Saudi Arabia. Tornados flew low-level airfield attacks in the 1991 Gulf War and later operations over Bosnia, Kosovo, Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya and Syria. The RAF retired its GR4s in 2019.

The wings sweep between 25 and 67 degrees, and the RB199 engines have thrust reversers.
engines: 2 x Turbo-Union RB199-34R Mk 103 afterburning turbofans

description:
The Bell 47 is a light piston-engined helicopter designed by Arthur M. Young and developed from Bell's Model 30 prototypes in the mid-1940s. It was built around a two-bladed main rotor with a stabiliser bar, a welded steel-tube fuselage and an open lattice tail boom, and on 8 March 1946 it became the first helicopter type certified for civil use.

Military examples served the US Army as the H-13 Sioux, flying observation, liaison and casualty evacuation missions in Korea and later in Vietnam; the British Army and the Italian, Japanese and some 30 other air arms also used the type. Production ran from 1946 to 1974, with more than 5,600 built by Bell and by licensees Agusta in Italy, Kawasaki in Japan and Westland in Britain.

The best known version, the 47G, carries a moulded plexiglass bubble canopy, exposed tube tailboom and external saddle fuel tanks.

The MB-326 is a single-engine, two-seat jet trainer and light attack aircraft designed by Ermanno Bazzocchi at Aermacchi in Italy. Begun as a private venture in the mid-1950s and first flown on 10 December 1957, it was intended for all-through jet training, taking a pupil from first solo to operational readiness on one airframe, powered by a licence-built Rolls-Royce Viper turbojet.

The Italian Air Force adopted it in 1962, and it became one of the most widely exported trainers of its generation, serving with more than ten air forces. About 800 were built, many under licence: Commonwealth Aircraft Corporation in Australia, Embraer in Brazil as the AT-26 Xavante, and Atlas in South Africa as the Impala. Armed Impalas flew ground attack missions in the South African Border War.

Straight wings with permanently fitted tip tanks and a long tandem canopy distinguish it from later swept-wing trainers.

The C-130 Hercules is a four-engined turboprop tactical transport designed by Lockheed to a February 1951 US Air Force requirement for an aircraft able to carry troops and cargo into short, unpaved forward strips. The layout set the pattern for military airlifters: a high wing, a pressurised box-section cargo hold at truck-bed height and a rear loading ramp. The prototype first flew on 23 August 1954 and deliveries began in December 1956.

Over 2,700 have been built in more than 40 variants, serving upwards of 60 nations in transport, aerial refuelling, gunship, weather reconnaissance, search and rescue and electronic warfare roles. It flew in Vietnam, the 1976 Entebbe raid, the Falklands and both Gulf wars.

Continuous production since 1954 makes it the longest-produced military aircraft in history.

The Piper J-3 Cub is a two-seat, high-wing, strut-braced light monoplane of welded steel tube and fabric construction, developed from the Taylor E-2 by C.G. Taylor and Walter Jamouneau and put into production by Piper Aircraft in 1938. It was built as a cheap, forgiving trainer, most often with a 65 hp Continental flat-four driving a fixed-pitch wooden propeller, and flown solo from the rear seat.

Around 20,000 were produced before the line closed in 1947. Roughly three quarters of American pilots trained under the wartime Civilian Pilot Training Program learned on Cubs, and 5,413 were taken by the US Army as the L-4 Grasshopper for artillery spotting, liaison and casualty evacuation in Europe and the Pacific.

The exposed cylinder heads either side of the cowling identify a genuine J-3.

The B-25 Mitchell is a twin-engined medium bomber developed by North American Aviation from its NA-40 design to meet a 1939 US Army Air Corps requirement. It combined a shoulder-mounted gull wing, tricycle undercarriage and twin fins, and first flew on 19 August 1940. The type was named for air power advocate Billy Mitchell.

It entered service in 1941 and fought in every theatre of the Second World War, flying level bombing, anti-shipping and low-level strafing missions; sixteen B-25Bs launched from the carrier Hornet for the Doolittle raid on Japan in April 1942. Britain, the Soviet Union, the Netherlands, China, Australia and Brazil all operated the type. Production reached 9,816 aircraft, the last retiring from Indonesian service in 1974.

Late J-model gunships carried up to eighteen .50 calibre machine guns in the nose and fuselage packs.
engines: 2 x Wright R-2600-92 Twin Cyclone radials

description:
The Wessex is a turbine-powered development of the Sikorsky S-58, built under licence in Britain by Westland. Westland replaced the American design's nose-mounted piston engine with turboshafts, which cut vibration and raised payload, and adapted the airframe to a Royal Navy requirement for a helicopter able to carry search radar and torpedoes on the same sortie.

Royal Navy HAS.1 anti-submarine aircraft entered service in 1961, followed by RAF HC.2 transports and HU.5 commando carriers. 382 were built. Wessexes flew in the Indonesia-Malaysia Confrontation, in Northern Ireland, and in the 1982 Falklands campaign, where about 55 HU.5s landed troops and stores and nine were lost. Australia, Ghana, Iraq and Uruguay operated export machines. British service ended in 2003.

The twin Gnome installation gives a downward-angled nose with exhaust stubs on each side of the forward fuselage, the clearest external difference from its Sikorsky parent.
engines: 2 x de Havilland Gnome H.1200 turboshafts

description:
The Mi-4 is a piston-engined transport helicopter designed by the Mil bureau in response to American helicopter operations in the Korean War and to the Sikorsky H-19. It repeats that layout, with a radial engine in the nose driving a shaft up to the rotor and the cockpit set above it, but is substantially larger, carrying 16 troops or 1,600 kg of cargo loaded through clamshell rear doors.

First flown on 3 June 1952 and in service from 1953, it became the standard Soviet assault and utility helicopter and remained in production until 1979; more than 4,000 were built including Chinese Harbin Z-5 licence aircraft. Exports went to some 30 air forces. Indian Mi-4s carried out air-assault landings in the 1971 Bangladesh war, and civil examples flew Arctic supply, survey and firefighting work.

Armed versions carried a ventral gondola for a machine gun and a bomb aimer.

The 737 is a short-haul jet airliner Boeing developed from 1964 to sit below the 727 on thin routes. Joe Sutter's team hung the engines directly under the wing instead of on the tail, which lightened the structure, and reused the 707 and 727 fuselage cross-section to keep six-abreast seating and existing tooling. Low ground clearance was deliberate, letting airlines load the aircraft without ground equipment.

First flown on 9 April 1967 and in service with Lufthansa from 10 February 1968, it has run through four generations: Original, Classic, Next Generation and MAX. More than 12,500 have been delivered, making it the most-produced jet airliner. Military derivatives include the P-8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft.

Early -100 and -200 aircraft carry long, slim engine nacelles; CFM56-powered Classic and later aircraft have flat-bottomed nacelles adopted to regain ground clearance.

The Su-24 is a two-seat, variable-sweep tactical bomber developed by Sukhoi from a 1961 requirement for an all-weather precision strike aircraft to succeed the Su-7B. Its Puma navigation and attack system, combining terrain-following radar, twin attack radars and a digital computer, was the first integrated system of its kind in Soviet service and allowed low-level attack at night. Pilot and weapons systems operator sit side by side.

The swing-wing T-6-2I flew on 17 January 1970 and the type entered service in 1974; about 1,400 were built. Su-24s flew interdiction sorties in Afghanistan, Chechnya, Georgia in 2008 and Syria from 2015, and have been used by both sides in Ukraine. Export operators included Iraq, Libya, Syria, Algeria and Iran, which retained Iraqi aircraft flown there in 1991.

The wings sweep between 16 and 69 degrees, the fixed inner gloves carrying the main landing gear.

The F-15 is a twin-engine air superiority fighter designed by McDonnell Douglas for a US Air Force requirement written after air combat over Vietnam exposed the limits of aircraft optimised for missile interception. The specification called for thrust exceeding weight, a large wing for sustained turning performance and a pulse-Doppler radar able to track targets below the horizon; ground attack equipment was deliberately left out of the original design.

First flown on 27 July 1972 and operational from 1976, 1,198 A/B/C/D and Japanese J/DJ aircraft were built, Mitsubishi assembling the F-15J under licence. Israel, Japan and Saudi Arabia were the principal export operators. The type is credited with over 100 air-to-air victories without a loss in air combat, including 41 Syrian aircraft over Lebanon in 1982.

The wing is very large for the aircraft's size, giving low wing loading, and the engines sit in widely spaced nacelles under a flat-topped fuselage.
engines: 2 x Pratt & Whitney F100-PW-220 afterburning turbofans

description:
The S-2 Tracker was a carrier-borne anti-submarine aircraft designed by Grumman for the United States Navy in the early 1950s. It was the first single airframe to combine submarine detection and attack, replacing the paired hunter-killer AF Guardians that had needed two aircraft to do the same job. The high-wing layout and two piston radials gave the endurance and low-speed handling required for long patrols from small carriers.

First flown on 4 December 1952 and in service from February 1954, 1,284 were built, with a further 99 assembled in Canada by de Havilland Canada as the CS2F. US Navy operations ended in 1976, but exports to Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Japan, the Netherlands, Taiwan and Turkey kept the type flying.

A retractable magnetic anomaly detector boom in the tail, a ventral search radome and wings that fold upward over the fuselage identify the type. Many surplus airframes were converted into aerial firefighting tankers, which is why so many survive.

The Gnat was a lightweight subsonic jet fighter designed at Folland by W. E. W. Petter around the argument that a small, cheap airframe with a single Orpheus turbojet could do the work of heavier and far more expensive fighters. The Royal Air Force bought it not as a fighter but as the two-seat Gnat T.1 advanced trainer, with a longer fuselage and revised wing.

A total of 449 were built, including licence production by Hindustan Aeronautics in India, which became the largest operator. HAL later developed the Ajeet, of which 89 were completed, first flying in 1975. Indian Gnats fought in the 1965 and 1971 wars with Pakistan and were credited with kills against F-86 Sabres. Finland took 13 and Yugoslavia two. The RAF's Red Arrows flew Gnats from 1965 to 1979; India withdrew the Ajeet in 1991.

Size is the distinguishing feature: 9.07 m long with a 6.76 m span.

The A-37 Dragonfly is a light attack aircraft developed from the Cessna T-37 trainer to give the United States Air Force a cheap counter-insurgency type for the war in Vietnam. The structure was strengthened for higher load factors, J85 turbojets replaced the trainer's smaller J69s, and eight underwing pylons, a 7.62 mm minigun, wingtip tanks and cockpit armour were added.

First flown in October 1964, it entered combat in 1967 under the Combat Dragon evaluation at Bien Hoa. 577 were built between 1963 and 1975, flying over 160,000 sorties for the loss of 22 USAF aircraft. More than 200 went to the South Vietnamese Air Force and about 95 were captured in 1975. Exports followed to Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras, Peru, South Korea, Thailand and Uruguay, and small numbers remain in Latin American service.

The side-by-side cockpit inherited from the T-37, the permanent wingtip tanks and the short tricycle undercarriage set it apart from other attack jets.

The F-14 Tomcat is a carrier-based variable-geometry fleet defence fighter, designed by Grumman after the US Navy abandoned the F-111B. Its task was to intercept Soviet bombers and anti-ship missiles far from the carrier group, using the AWG-9 radar and the AIM-54 Phoenix missile, a combination able to track 24 targets and engage six simultaneously.

First flown in December 1970 and in service from 1974, it replaced the F-4 Phantom II in Navy squadrons. 712 were built. Crews shot down Libyan aircraft over the Gulf of Sidra in 1981 and 1989, and the type later flew strike and TARPS reconnaissance missions over Iraq and Afghanistan before US retirement in September 2006. Iran received 79 aircraft before the 1979 revolution and still flies a small number.

The flat load-bearing area between the widely spaced engine nacelles, the twin canted fins and the wing gloves make it recognisable at a distance.
engines: 2 x Pratt & Whitney TF30-P-414A afterburning turbofans

description:
The T-38 Talon is a twin-engine supersonic advanced trainer, the first aircraft of that kind to enter service. Northrop developed it from the company-funded N-156 design that also produced the F-5 fighter, aiming to teach high-speed handling at a fraction of the cost of converting a frontline fighter into a trainer.

First flown in 1959 and in United States Air Force service from 1961, 1,187 were built before production ended in 1972. It remains the Air Force's principal advanced trainer in upgraded T-38C form, feeding pilots to the F-15, F-16, F-22, F-35 and bomber fleets. NASA flies a fleet from Ellington Field for astronaut proficiency and chase duties. Germany, Turkey, Portugal, South Korea and Taiwan also operated the type.

The thin sharp-edged wing, area-ruled fuselage and stepped tandem canopies distinguish it from later trainers.
engines: 2 x General Electric J85-GE-5A afterburning turbojets

description:
The Curtiss P-40 was a single-seat fighter and fighter-bomber, developed in 1937 from the radial-engined P-36 Hawk by substituting a liquid-cooled Allison V-1710 inline engine. The prototype XP-40 first flew on 14 October 1938. It was the only modern American fighter available in quantity when the United States entered the war in December 1941.

Curtiss built 13,738 examples at Buffalo, New York, between 1939 and November 1944. The type served with some 28 nations: as the Tomahawk and Kittyhawk with RAF and Commonwealth squadrons in North Africa, with the American Volunteer Group in China, and in large numbers with the Soviet air force under Lend-Lease. Brazil retired its last examples in 1958.

The Allison engine lacked a two-stage supercharger, limiting performance above roughly 4,500 m, but below that the aircraft was fast, rugged and effective in ground attack. The long carburettor intake above the nose distinguishes Allison-powered variants from the Merlin-engined P-40F and P-40L.

The Sukhoi Su-27 is a twin-engine supersonic air-superiority fighter developed against the Soviet PFI requirement of 1969, which sought a counter to the American F-15. The first T-10 prototype flew on 20 May 1977; the design fell short of its targets and was substantially rebuilt as the T-10S, which flew in 1981. Service entry followed in June 1985.

Around 680 were built, principally at Komsomolsk-on-Amur. The type equipped Soviet air-defence and frontal-aviation regiments and passed after 1991 to Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, with exports to China, Vietnam, Ethiopia, Angola and Indonesia. China has built it under licence as the Shenyang J-11 since 1998. It remains in service and underpins the Su-30, Su-33, Su-34 and Su-35.

The blended wing-body, widely spaced engine nacelles and the tail boom between them are characteristic; large internal fuel capacity gives an unrefuelled range of about 3,500 km.

The Messerschmitt Bf 109 is a single-seat fighter designed by Willy Messerschmitt at Bayerische Flugzeugwerke to a 1934 requirement for a monoplane interceptor. It combined all-metal stressed-skin construction, an enclosed cockpit, retractable undercarriage and leading-edge slats on the smallest airframe that would carry the Junkers Jumo, later Daimler-Benz, engine. The prototype flew in 1935 and the type entered service in 1937.

About 34,000 were completed, more than any other fighter. It was tested in Spain by the Condor Legion and fought in the Battle of Britain, over the Eastern Front and in the defence of Germany until 1945, also serving with Finland, Hungary, Romania, Italy, Bulgaria, Switzerland and Croatia. Production continued postwar: Avia built the Jumo-powered S-199 in Czechoslovakia, some reaching Israel in 1948, and Hispano Aviacion built the HA-1112, flown by Spain until 1965.

The narrow-track undercarriage, hinged to the fuselage rather than the wing, caused heavy landing accident losses and remains the type's most recognisable feature.

The Antonov An-24 is a twin-turboprop short-haul airliner designed at Kiev from 1957 to replace the Li-2, Il-14 and An-2 on Aeroflot regional routes. A high wing, low-pressure tyres and an onboard auxiliary power unit allow operation from unpaved strips and unprepared airfields in the Arctic and Central Asia. It first flew on 29 October 1959 and entered service in 1962.

More than 1,360 were built at Kiev, Ulan-Ude and Irkutsk, seating up to 50 passengers. Aeroflot was the principal operator, and the type was exported across the Eastern Bloc, Africa, Cuba and Asia. China produced a reverse-engineered development as the Xian Y-7. Military examples served as transports, navigator trainers and ice-reconnaissance aircraft, and a small number remain in commercial service.

Direct descendants include the An-26 with a rear loading ramp and the An-30 aerial survey aircraft with a glazed nose.

The AT-26 Xavante is a two-seat jet trainer and light attack aircraft, the Brazilian licence-built version of the Italian Aermacchi MB-326G. Embraer signed the manufacturing agreement with Aermacchi in 1970, and the first Brazilian-assembled aircraft, company designation EMB-326GB, flew on 3 September 1971 - the first jet built in Brazil.

Embraer completed 182 aircraft. Of these, 167 went to the Forca Aerea Brasileira for advanced flying training, weapons instruction and counter-insurgency work; six were delivered to Togo and nine to Paraguay, and eleven ex-Brazilian machines went to the Argentine Navy in 1983. The FAB withdrew the type on 2 December 2010 after 39 years, replaced by the AMX and the A-29 Super Tucano.

Straight wings with permanent tip tanks and a single Viper turbojet in the rear fuselage identify the family; armed versions carry six underwing hardpoints.
